FunctionInfo.Title: Kronecker tensor product
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
Matrix KroneckerProduct<T>(Matrix mactrices1, Matrix mactrices2, ...)

Forms a block matrix by replacing each entry of the left operand with that entry times the right operand.

Definition / convention: (A⊗B) block (i,j)=AᵢⱼB.

Arguments / value: Nonempty inputs for indexed left-fold implementations; elementwise operations require equal dimensions.

Important: At least one compatible matrix; folds left to right. Matrix dimensions multiply, so memory grows quickly.

Reference: github.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Kronecker sum
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
Matrix KroneckerSum<T>(Matrix mactrices1, Matrix mactrices2, ...)

Combines independent linear operators on a tensor-product space.

Definition / convention: A⊕B=A⊗I+I⊗B.

Arguments / value: Nonempty inputs for indexed left-fold implementations; elementwise operations require equal dimensions.

Important: Use square matrices for the standard definition; folds left to right. This is not the block-diagonal direct sum.

Reference: github.com

FunctionInfo.Title: LU factorization object
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
LU`1 LU<T>(Matrix M)

Pivoted lower/upper triangular factorization.

Definition / convention: A = P·L·U, subject to the factorization object’s permutation convention.

Arguments / value: Square matrix for the usual LU solve/determinant operations.

Important: Returns a factorization object exposing factors and solve/diagnostic operations; it is not just one factor matrix.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Laguerre polynomial
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real Laguerre(integer n, real x)

A degree-n polynomial orthogonal on [0,∞) with weight x^α exp(−x).

Definition / convention: Lₙ^(α)(x)=Σₖ₌₀ⁿ (−1)ᵏ C(n+α,n−k)xᵏ/k!

Arguments / value: Integer n≥0. This overload fixes α=0.

Important: The argument x is an evaluation coordinate, not an index.

Example: Laguerre(1,2) = -1

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Generalized Laguerre polynomial
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real Laguerre(integer n, real α, real x)

A degree-n polynomial orthogonal on [0,∞) with weight x^α exp(−x).

Definition / convention: Lₙ^(α)(x)=Σₖ₌₀ⁿ (−1)ᵏ C(n+α,n−k)xᵏ/k!

Arguments / value: Integer n≥0. The general wrapper requires α>−1.

Important: The argument x is an evaluation coordinate, not an index.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Lambert W, real branch 0
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real LambertW0(real x)

Inverts the map w↦w·exp(w), selecting one branch.

Definition / convention: W(x)·exp(W(x))=x.

Arguments / value: The principal real branch has x≥−1/e and W≥−1.

Important: This wrapper rejects x=−1/e as well as smaller inputs, although the mathematical endpoint is W=−1.

Example: LambertW0(0) = 0

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Lambert W, real branch −1
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real LambertWm1(real x)

Inverts the map w↦w·exp(w), selecting one branch.

Definition / convention: W(x)·exp(W(x))=x.

Arguments / value: The negative real branch has x∈[−1/e,0) and W≤−1.

Important: This wrapper rejects x=−1/e as well as smaller inputs, although the mathematical endpoint is W=−1. For positive x, GSL’s W₋₁ routine returns its W₀ continuation; that is not a real negative-branch value.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Landau–Ramanujan constant
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real LandauRamanujanConstant

Coefficient in the count of positive integers expressible as a sum of two integer squares.

Definition / convention: Count≤x ~ K·x/sqrt(ln x).

Arguments / value: Stored application value: 0.7642236535892206. Dimensionless.

Important: Counts represented integers once, not their number of different representations. This is the finite stored binary64 approximation, not an arbitrary-precision evaluation of the defining limit, series or construction.

Reference: oeis.org

FunctionInfo.Title: Laplace (double exponential) — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real Laplace.CDF(real location, real scale, real x)

Returns F(x)=P(X≤x), the accumulated probability through x. A symmetric distribution with an exponential tail on each side of its location.

Definition / convention: f(x)=exp(−|x−location|/scale)/(2·scale); Var[X]=2·scale².

Arguments / value: location is real; scale>0; x is real. Scale is not the standard deviation.

Important: This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one.

Example: Laplace.CDF(0,1,0) = 0.5.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Description:

Returns a Boolean indicating whether the parameter set passes the library’s validity check; it does not compute a sample or a probability. A symmetric distribution with an exponential tail on each side of its location.

Definition / convention: f(x)=exp(−|x−location|/scale)/(2·scale); Var[X]=2·scale².

Arguments / value: location is real; scale>0; x is real. Scale is not the standard deviation.

Important: This precheck is not proof of numerical convergence, finite moments, finite precision, or support of every operation. Prefer the finite, nondegenerate model conditions given here, even where the library accepts a limiting case.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Description:

Probability density f(x). A symmetric distribution with an exponential tail on each side of its location.

Definition / convention: f(x)=exp(−|x−location|/scale)/(2·scale); Var[X]=2·scale².

Arguments / value: location is real; scale>0; x is real. Scale is not the standard deviation. Evaluate at x; the support is specified above.

Important: A density is not P(X=x): point probability is zero for a continuous law. Integrate the density over an interval to obtain a probability.

Example: Laplace.CDF(0,1,0) = 0.5.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

Arguments / value: location is real; scale>0; x is real. Scale is not the standard deviation. Evaluate at x; the support is specified above.

FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real LaplaceLimitConstantλ

Eccentricity threshold for convergence of the classical eccentricity power series used in Kepler’s equation.

Definition / convention: λ·exp(sqrt(1+λ²))/(1+sqrt(1+λ²))=1; λ>0.

Arguments / value: Stored application value: 0.6627434193491816. Dimensionless.

Important: This concerns that series, not the existence of a solution to Kepler’s equation. This is the finite stored binary64 approximation, not an arbitrary-precision evaluation of the defining limit, series or construction.

Reference: oeis.org

FunctionInfo.Title: Silicon lattice parameter
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real LatticeParameterOfSilicon

Cubic unit-cell edge length for the reference silicon crystal.

Definition / convention: a(Si).

Arguments / value: Unit: m. Stored application value: 5.431020504E-10.

Important: Crystal conditions and isotope composition matter; use the source reference conditions for precision diffraction. The stored value is the application’s legacy binary64 value, not a live CODATA lookup or an uncertainty-bearing measurement. Use the cited current NIST/SI definition for precision work; independently stored related constants may not be numerically consistent.

Reference: physics.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Radial eigenfunction on three-dimensional hyperbolic space
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real LegendreH3D(integer l, real λ, real η)

A regular radial eigenfunction of the Laplacian on H³ in the GSL normalization.

Definition / convention: For l=0: sin(λη)/(λsinhη), with continuous limits.

Arguments / value: Integer l≥0, radial coordinate η≥0, real spectral parameter λ. This wrapper rejects λ=0 for l≥2.

Important: This is a hyperbolic-space radial function, not an ordinary Legendre polynomial evaluated at η.

Reference: www.gnu.org

FunctionInfo.Title: Associated Legendre function
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real LegendreP(integer l, integer m, real x)

An associated angular-momentum function built by differentiating a Legendre polynomial.

Definition / convention: P_l^m(x)=(−1)^m(1−x²)^(m/2) dᵐP_l(x)/dxᵐ for m≥0.

Arguments / value: Integer l≥0, −1≤x≤1 in this wrapper. Integer |m|≤l; negative orders use the standard factorial relation.

Important: Includes the Condon–Shortley phase (−1)^m; this is not spherical-harmonic normalization.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Legendre polynomial
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real LegendreP(integer l, real x)

The degree-l solution of Legendre’s equation normalized to P_l(1)=1.

Definition / convention: P_l(x)=1/(2ˡl!) dˡ[(x²−1)ˡ]/dxˡ.

Arguments / value: Integer l≥0, −1≤x≤1 in this wrapper.

Example: LegendreP(2,0) = -0.5

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Legendre function of the second kind
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real LegendreQ(integer l, real x)

The real second solution of Legendre’s equation, singular at the interval endpoints.

Definition / convention: Q₀(x)=0.5·ln|(1+x)/(1−x)|

Arguments / value: Integer l≥0; this wrapper permits x>−1 except x=1. It uses the real GSL convention on either side of 1.

Important: This is not the Legendre polynomial P_l and is not complex analytic continuation across the cut.

Reference: www.gnu.org

FunctionInfo.Title: Lemniscate constant
FunctionInfo.Description:

real LemniscateConstantL

Twice the basic lemniscatic quarter-period integral.

Definition / convention: L=2∫₀¹ dt/sqrt(1−t⁴)=Γ(1/4)²/(2sqrt(2π)).

Arguments / value: Stored application value: 2.6220575542921196. Dimensionless.

Important: The normalization is L≈2.62205755; FirstLemniscateConstantLA stores half this value. This is the finite stored binary64 approximation, not an arbitrary-precision evaluation of the defining limit, series or construction.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Liouville’s constant
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax

Decimal with ones at factorial-numbered positions and zeros elsewhere.

Definition / convention: L=Σ(n=1..∞)10^(−n!).

Arguments / value: Stored application value: 0.110001. Dimensionless.

Important: The stored binary64 value cannot retain the isolated digits arbitrarily far into the decimal expansion. This is the finite stored binary64 approximation, not an arbitrary-precision evaluation of the defining limit, series or construction.

FunctionInfo.Title: Lochs’ constant
FunctionInfo.Description:

real LochConstant

Typical number of regular continued-fraction terms determined per base-ten digit.

Definition / convention: 6 ln2 ln10/π².

Arguments / value: Stored application value: 0.9702701143920339. Dimensionless.

Important: The identifier omits the final s in Lochs. ContinuedFractionsConstant is its reciprocal. This is the finite stored binary64 approximation, not an arbitrary-precision evaluation of the defining limit, series or construction.

FunctionInfo.Title: Lognormal — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real LogNormal.CDF(real mu, real sigma, real x)

Returns F(x)=P(X≤x), the accumulated probability through x. A positive variable whose natural logarithm is normally distributed.

Definition / convention: ln X~Normal(mu,sigma²); f(x)=exp(−(ln x−mu)²/(2sigma²))/(x·sigma·sqrt(2π)).

Arguments / value: mu is the mean of ln X; sigma>0 is the STANDARD DEVIATION of ln X; x>0.

Important: mu and sigma are not the mean and standard deviation of X. E[X]=exp(mu+sigma²/2); sigma=0 is a degenerate limit supported by some library paths. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one.

Example: LogNormal.CDF(0,1,1) = 0.5.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Lognormal — Estimate distribution parameters
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
LogNormal LogNormal.Estimate(IEnumerable`1 samples, Random randomSource)

Fits a distribution object to the supplied sample sequence. A positive variable whose natural logarithm is normally distributed.

Definition / convention: ln X~Normal(mu,sigma²); f(x)=exp(−(ln x−mu)²/(2sigma²))/(x·sigma·sqrt(2π)).

Arguments / value: samples is a finite, nonempty data sequence; randomSource configures subsequent draws, not the fitting data. Use enough nondegenerate observations to estimate the spread.

Important: mu and sigma are not the mean and standard deviation of X. E[X]=exp(mu+sigma²/2); sigma=0 is a degenerate limit supported by some library paths. Every observation must be positive. The implementation fits a normal law to natural logarithms of the data; it does not fit a Gaussian directly to the original observations.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Lognormal — Inverse CDF (quantile)
FunctionInfo.Description:

Definition / convention: ln X~Normal(mu,sigma²); f(x)=exp(−(ln x−mu)²/(2sigma²))/(x·sigma·sqrt(2π)).

Arguments / value: mu is the mean of ln X; sigma>0 is the STANDARD DEVIATION of ln X; x>0. The argument p/probability is a cumulative probability in [0,1], not another shape parameter.

Important: mu and sigma are not the mean and standard deviation of X. E[X]=exp(mu+sigma²/2); sigma=0 is a degenerate limit supported by some library paths. Interior probabilities 0<p<1 avoid infinite endpoints for unbounded distributions. Numerical inversion has finite accuracy.

Example: LogNormal.CDF(0,1,1) = 0.5.

Definition / convention: ln X~Normal(mu,sigma²); f(x)=exp(−(ln x−mu)²/(2sigma²))/(x·sigma·sqrt(2π)).

FunctionInfo.Title: Matrix normal — Parameter validity check
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
bool MatrixNormal.IsValidParameterSet(Matrix m, Matrix v, Matrix k)

Returns a Boolean indicating whether the parameter set passes the library’s validity check; it does not compute a sample or a probability. A Gaussian distribution over matrices with separable row and column covariance.

Definition / convention: vec(X)~Normal(vec(m), k⊗v), using column-stacked vec.

Arguments / value: m is the d×p mean matrix; v is d×d row covariance; k is p×p column covariance. Covariance matrices must be symmetric positive definite.

Important: Matrix shapes are part of the contract; m is a matrix of means, not a scalar dimension. The covariance of vectorized samples is a Kronecker product, not v+k. This precheck is not proof of numerical convergence, finite moments, finite precision, or support of every operation. Prefer the finite, nondegenerate model conditions given here, even where the library accepts a limiting case.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Matrix normal — One random draw
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
Matrix MatrixNormal.Sample(Random rnd, Matrix m, Matrix v, Matrix k)

Returns one random draw. A Gaussian distribution over matrices with separable row and column covariance.

Definition / convention: vec(X)~Normal(vec(m), k⊗v), using column-stacked vec.

Arguments / value: m is the d×p mean matrix; v is d×d row covariance; k is p×p column covariance. Covariance matrices must be symmetric positive definite. rnd is a non-null System.Random instance; its state advances as draws are made.

Important: Matrix shapes are part of the contract; m is a matrix of means, not a scalar dimension. The covariance of vectorized samples is a Kronecker product, not v+k. Sample values are random, not the density/CDF evaluated at the parameters. Reproducibility requires an explicit generator and a controlled sequence of calls; these are not cryptographic random sources. IMPORTANT: Math.NET 5.0 sampling does not implement the stated column-covariance convention. It builds v⊗k⁻¹ and unpacks the draw by columns, instead of using k⊗v. In the 1×1 case with m=0, v=1 and k=4, the actual sample variance is 1/4, not the intended 4. Do not use this sampler as if k were the advertised column covariance; the formula above describes the mathematical model, not this implementation defect.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Negative binomial — failures — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real NegativeBinomial.CDF(real r, real p, real x)

Returns F(x)=P(X≤x), the accumulated probability through x. The number of failures before r successes; the gamma-function extension also permits positive real r.

Definition / convention: P(X=k)=Γ(k+r)/(Γ(r)·k!) · p^r(1−p)^k, k=0,1,… .

Arguments / value: r>0, 0<p≤1 for the ordinary law; k is a nonnegative integer. p is the success probability.

Important: E[X]=r(1−p)/p. This counts failures, unlike this library’s Geometric class, which counts trials including the first success. Boundary r=0 or p=0 needs separate limiting interpretation. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one. For a discrete law, the mathematical CDF is a step function over integer outcomes; use integer x at jumps. Fractional-x behavior must not be used as a continuous interpolation of probability masses.

Example: NegativeBinomial.PMF(1,0.5,0) = 0.5.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Negative binomial — failures — Parameter validity check
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax

Returns a Boolean indicating whether the parameter set passes the library’s validity check; it does not compute a sample or a probability. The number of failures before r successes; the gamma-function extension also permits positive real r.

Definition / convention: P(X=k)=Γ(k+r)/(Γ(r)·k!) · p^r(1−p)^k, k=0,1,… .

Arguments / value: r>0, 0<p≤1 for the ordinary law; k is a nonnegative integer. p is the success probability.

Important: E[X]=r(1−p)/p. This counts failures, unlike this library’s Geometric class, which counts trials including the first success. Boundary r=0 or p=0 needs separate limiting interpretation. This precheck is not proof of numerical convergence, finite moments, finite precision, or support of every operation. Prefer the finite, nondegenerate model conditions given here, even where the library accepts a limiting case.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

Important: E[X]=r(1−p)/p. This counts failures, unlike this library’s Geometric class, which counts trials including the first success. Boundary r=0 or p=0 needs separate limiting interpretation. A mass is a point probability between 0 and 1.

Example: NegativeBinomial.PMF(1,0.5,0) = 0.5.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

Definition / convention: P(X=k)=Γ(k+r)/(Γ(r)·k!) · p^r(1−p)^k, k=0,1,… .

Arguments / value: r>0, 0<p≤1 for the ordinary law; k is a nonnegative integer. p is the success probability. Evaluate at integer k in the stated support.

Important: E[X]=r(1−p)/p. This counts failures, unlike this library’s Geometric class, which counts trials including the first success. Boundary r=0 or p=0 needs separate limiting interpretation. This is a natural logarithm of the mass/density, not the probability of a logarithmically transformed variable. Zero mass/density has logarithm −∞; direct log evaluation can avoid ordinary underflow.

FunctionInfo.Title: Normal (Gaussian) — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real Normal.CDF(real mean, real stddev, real x)

Returns F(x)=P(X≤x), the accumulated probability through x. A symmetric bell-shaped distribution about its mean. The width is the standard deviation, not the variance.

Definition / convention: f(x)=exp(−(x−μ)²/(2σ²))/(σ·sqrt(2π)); E[X]=μ; Var[X]=σ².

Arguments / value: mean=μ is real; stddev=σ>0; x is real.

Important: A zero standard deviation is a degenerate point mass accepted by some library paths; ordinary density formulas assume σ>0. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one.

Example: Normal.CDF(0,1,0) = 0.5; Normal.InvCDF(0,1,0.5) = 0.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Normal (Gaussian) — Estimate distribution parameters
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
Normal Normal.Estimate(IEnumerable`1 samples, Random randomSource)

Fits a distribution object to the supplied sample sequence. A symmetric bell-shaped distribution about its mean. The width is the standard deviation, not the variance.

Definition / convention: f(x)=exp(−(x−μ)²/(2σ²))/(σ·sqrt(2π)); E[X]=μ; Var[X]=σ².

Arguments / value: samples is a finite, nonempty data sequence; randomSource configures subsequent draws, not the fitting data. Use enough nondegenerate observations to estimate the spread.

Important: A zero standard deviation is a degenerate point mass accepted by some library paths; ordinary density formulas assume σ>0. The implementation uses the sample mean and sample standard deviation; it is not a general robust fit or a claim that the data are Gaussian.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Normal (Gaussian) — Inverse CDF (quantile)
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real Normal.InvCDF(real mean, real stddev, real p)

Maps cumulative probability to the corresponding outcome threshold. A symmetric bell-shaped distribution about its mean. The width is the standard deviation, not the variance.

Definition / convention: f(x)=exp(−(x−μ)²/(2σ²))/(σ·sqrt(2π)); E[X]=μ; Var[X]=σ².

Arguments / value: mean=μ is real; stddev=σ>0; x is real. The argument p/probability is a cumulative probability in [0,1], not another shape parameter.

Important: A zero standard deviation is a degenerate point mass accepted by some library paths; ordinary density formulas assume σ>0. Interior probabilities 0<p<1 avoid infinite endpoints for unbounded distributions. Numerical inversion has finite accuracy.

Example: Normal.CDF(0,1,0) = 0.5; Normal.InvCDF(0,1,0.5) = 0.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

Definition / convention: f(x)=exp(−(x−μ)²/(2σ²))/(σ·sqrt(2π)); E[X]=μ; Var[X]=σ².

Arguments / value: mean=μ is real; stddev=σ>0; x is real. Evaluate at x; the support is specified above.

Important: A zero standard deviation is a degenerate point mass accepted by some library paths; ordinary density formulas assume σ>0. A density is not P(X=x): point probability is zero for a continuous law. Integrate the density over an interval to obtain a probability.

FunctionInfo.Title: Pareto — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real Pareto.CDF(real scale, real shape, real x)

Returns F(x)=P(X≤x), the accumulated probability through x. A heavy-tailed positive distribution with a hard lower cutoff.

Definition / convention: f(x)=shape·scale^shape/x^(shape+1), x≥scale.

Arguments / value: scale>0 is the MINIMUM value; shape>0 controls tail decay.

Important: The mean needs shape>1 and variance needs shape>2. The parameter order is scale,shape here, unlike Weibull’s shape,scale. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one.

Example: Pareto.CDF(1,2,2) = 0.75.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Pareto — Inverse CDF (quantile)
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real Pareto.InvCDF(real scale, real shape, real p)

Maps cumulative probability to the corresponding outcome threshold. A heavy-tailed positive distribution with a hard lower cutoff.

Definition / convention: f(x)=shape·scale^shape/x^(shape+1), x≥scale.

Arguments / value: scale>0 is the MINIMUM value; shape>0 controls tail decay. The argument p/probability is a cumulative probability in [0,1], not another shape parameter.

Important: The mean needs shape>1 and variance needs shape>2. The parameter order is scale,shape here, unlike Weibull’s shape,scale. Interior probabilities 0<p<1 avoid infinite endpoints for unbounded distributions. Numerical inversion has finite accuracy.

Example: Pareto.CDF(1,2,2) = 0.75.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

Returns a Boolean indicating whether the parameter set passes the library’s validity check; it does not compute a sample or a probability. A heavy-tailed positive distribution with a hard lower cutoff.

Definition / convention: f(x)=shape·scale^shape/x^(shape+1), x≥scale.

Arguments / value: scale>0 is the MINIMUM value; shape>0 controls tail decay.

Important: The mean needs shape>1 and variance needs shape>2. The parameter order is scale,shape here, unlike Weibull’s shape,scale. This precheck is not proof of numerical convergence, finite moments, finite precision, or support of every operation. Prefer the finite, nondegenerate model conditions given here, even where the library accepts a limiting case.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Pareto — Probability density f(x)
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real Pareto.PDF(real scale, real shape, real x)

Probability density f(x). A heavy-tailed positive distribution with a hard lower cutoff.

Definition / convention: f(x)=shape·scale^shape/x^(shape+1), x≥scale.

Arguments / value: scale>0 is the MINIMUM value; shape>0 controls tail decay. Evaluate at x; the support is specified above.

Important: The mean needs shape>1 and variance needs shape>2. The parameter order is scale,shape here, unlike Weibull’s shape,scale. A density is not P(X=x): point probability is zero for a continuous law. Integrate the density over an interval to obtain a probability.

Example: Pareto.CDF(1,2,2) = 0.75.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

Definition / convention: f(x)=shape·scale^shape/x^(shape+1), x≥scale.

Arguments / value: scale>0 is the MINIMUM value; shape>0 controls tail decay. Evaluate at x; the support is specified above.

Important: The mean needs shape>1 and variance needs shape>2. The parameter order is scale,shape here, unlike Weibull’s shape,scale. This is a natural logarithm of the mass/density, not the probability of a logarithmically transformed variable. Zero mass/density has logarithm −∞; direct log evaluation can avoid ordinary underflow.

Example: Pareto.CDF(1,2,2) = 0.75.

Definition / convention: f(x)=shape·scale^shape/x^(shape+1), x≥scale.

Arguments / value: scale>0 is the MINIMUM value; shape>0 controls tail decay. rnd is a non-null System.Random instance; its state advances as draws are made.

Important: The mean needs shape>1 and variance needs shape>2. The parameter order is scale,shape here, unlike Weibull’s shape,scale. FunctionInfo.Title: Poisson — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real Poisson.CDF(real lambda, real x)

Returns F(x)=P(X≤x), the accumulated probability through x. A count model for independent events in a fixed exposure with a constant average rate.

Definition / convention: P(X=k)=exp(−λ)·λ^k/k!; E[X]=Var[X]=λ.

Arguments / value: lambda=λ>0 is the expected count in the exposure; k is a nonnegative integer.

Important: Specify the exposure separately in your model: λ is a count mean, not necessarily a rate per second. λ=0 has a mathematical point-mass limit but some library entry points require λ>0. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one. For a discrete law, the mathematical CDF is a step function over integer outcomes; use integer x at jumps. Fractional-x behavior must not be used as a continuous interpolation of probability masses.

Example: Poisson.PMF(1,0) = exp(−1).

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

Definition / convention: P(X=k)=exp(−λ)·λ^k/k!; E[X]=Var[X]=λ.

Arguments / value: lambda=λ>0 is the expected count in the exposure; k is a nonnegative integer. Evaluate at integer k in the stated support.

Important: Specify the exposure separately in your model: λ is a count mean, not necessarily a rate per second. λ=0 has a mathematical point-mass limit but some library entry points require λ>0. A mass is a point probability between 0 and 1.

Example: Poisson.PMF(1,0) = exp(−1).

FunctionInfo.Title: Rayleigh — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real Rayleigh.CDF(real scale, real x)

Returns F(x)=P(X≤x), the accumulated probability through x. The length of a two-dimensional vector of independent zero-mean normal components with equal standard deviation.

Definition / convention: f(x)=x·exp(−x²/(2scale²))/scale², x≥0.

Arguments / value: scale>0 is the standard deviation of EACH Gaussian component, not the mean radius.

Important: This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one.

Example: Rayleigh.CDF(1,1) = 1−exp(−0.5).

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Rayleigh — Inverse CDF (quantile)

Arguments / value: scale>0 is the standard deviation of EACH Gaussian component, not the mean radius. The argument p/probability is a cumulative probability in [0,1], not another shape parameter.

Important: Interior probabilities 0<p<1 avoid infinite endpoints for unbounded distributions. Numerical inversion has finite accuracy.

Example: Rayleigh.CDF(1,1) = 1−exp(−0.5).

Arguments / value: Integers n≥1, 0≤l<n, nuclear charge Z>0, radius r≥0 in atomic units. The full orbital is Rₙₗ(r)Yₗᵐ(θ,φ).

FunctionInfo.Title: Stable — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real Stable.CDF(real alpha, real beta, real scale, real location, real x)

Returns F(x)=P(X≤x), the accumulated probability through x. A heavy-tail family closed under sums up to location/scale changes; alpha controls the stability index and beta skewness.

Definition / convention: At alpha=2: Normal(location, stddev=sqrt(2)·scale). At alpha=1,beta=0: Cauchy(location,scale).

Arguments / value: 0<alpha≤2, −1≤beta≤1, scale>0; location is real.

Important: Do not interchange stable-law parameterizations blindly, especially when alpha=1 and beta≠0. The implemented sampler scales/shifts a standard draw; density/CDF support is more limited than sampling. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one. IMPORTANT: Math.NET 5.0 implements this evaluation only for alpha=2 (Gaussian), alpha=1 with beta=0 (Cauchy), or alpha=0.5 with beta=1 (Lévy). Other stable parameters throw NotSupportedException even though sampling and IsValidParameterSet accept them. For the Lévy branch, use x>location for ordinary evaluation. At x=location, PDF and PDFLn return NaN instead of their mathematical limits 0 and −∞; CDF returns 0. Below location, PDF/PDFLn throw and CDF returns NaN, although the mathematical density and CDF are zero there.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Stable — Parameter validity check
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax

Returns a Boolean indicating whether the parameter set passes the library’s validity check; it does not compute a sample or a probability. A heavy-tail family closed under sums up to location/scale changes; alpha controls the stability index and beta skewness.

Definition / convention: At alpha=2: Normal(location, stddev=sqrt(2)·scale). At alpha=1,beta=0: Cauchy(location,scale).

Arguments / value: 0<alpha≤2, −1≤beta≤1, scale>0; location is real.

Important: Do not interchange stable-law parameterizations blindly, especially when alpha=1 and beta≠0. The implemented sampler scales/shifts a standard draw; density/CDF support is more limited than sampling. This precheck is not proof of numerical convergence, finite moments, finite precision, or support of every operation. Prefer the finite, nondegenerate model conditions given here, even where the library accepts a limiting case.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Stable — Probability density f(x)

Arguments / value: 0<alpha≤2, −1≤beta≤1, scale>0; location is real. Evaluate at x; the support is specified above.

Important: Do not interchange stable-law parameterizations blindly, especially when alpha=1 and beta≠0. The implemented sampler scales/shifts a standard draw; density/CDF support is more limited than sampling. A density is not P(X=x): point probability is zero for a continuous law. Integrate the density over an interval to obtain a probability. IMPORTANT: Math.NET 5.0 implements this evaluation only for alpha=2 (Gaussian), alpha=1 with beta=0 (Cauchy), or alpha=0.5 with beta=1 (Lévy). Other stable parameters throw NotSupportedException even though sampling and IsValidParameterSet accept them. For the Lévy branch, use x>location for ordinary evaluation. At x=location, PDF and PDFLn return NaN instead of their mathematical limits 0 and −∞; CDF returns 0. Important: Do not interchange stable-law parameterizations blindly, especially when alpha=1 and beta≠0. The implemented sampler scales/shifts a standard draw; density/CDF support is more limited than sampling. This is a natural logarithm of the mass/density, not the probability of a logarithmically transformed variable. Zero mass/density has logarithm −∞; direct log evaluation can avoid ordinary underflow. IMPORTANT: Math.NET 5.0 implements this evaluation only for alpha=2 (Gaussian), alpha=1 with beta=0 (Cauchy), or alpha=0.5 with beta=1 (Lévy). Other stable parameters throw NotSupportedException even though sampling and IsValidParameterSet accept them. For the Lévy branch, use x>location for ordinary evaluation. The modified Struve solution of an inhomogeneous Bessel equation, distinct from modified Bessel I.

Definition / convention: L_ν(x)=Σₖ₌₀^∞ (x/2)^(2k+ν+1)/[Γ(k+3/2)Γ(k+ν+3/2)]

Arguments / value: Real x; this entry fixes ν=1. Large positive x gives rapid exponential growth.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Student t — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real StudentT.CDF(real location, real scale, real freedom, real x)

Returns F(x)=P(X≤x), the accumulated probability through x. A symmetric heavy-tailed location-scale t distribution, approaching a Gaussian as freedom grows.

Definition / convention: f(x)=Γ((ν+1)/2)/(scale·sqrt(νπ)Γ(ν/2)) · [1+((x−location)/scale)²/ν]^(−(ν+1)/2).

Arguments / value: freedom=ν>0; scale>0; location and x are real.

Important: Scale is not the standard deviation: Var[X]=scale²·ν/(ν−2) only for ν>2. The mean needs ν>1. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one.

Example: StudentT.CDF(0,1,3,0) = 0.5.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Student t — Inverse CDF (quantile)
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real StudentT.InvCDF(real location, real scale, real freedom, real p)

Maps cumulative probability to the corresponding outcome threshold. A symmetric heavy-tailed location-scale t distribution, approaching a Gaussian as freedom grows.

Definition / convention: f(x)=Γ((ν+1)/2)/(scale·sqrt(νπ)Γ(ν/2)) · [1+((x−location)/scale)²/ν]^(−(ν+1)/2).

Arguments / value: freedom=ν>0; scale>0; location and x are real. The argument p/probability is a cumulative probability in [0,1], not another shape parameter.

Important: Scale is not the standard deviation: Var[X]=scale²·ν/(ν−2) only for ν>2. The mean needs ν>1. Interior probabilities 0<p<1 avoid infinite endpoints for unbounded distributions. Numerical inversion has finite accuracy.

Example: StudentT.CDF(0,1,3,0) = 0.5.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Description:

Returns a Boolean indicating whether the parameter set passes the library’s validity check; it does not compute a sample or a probability. A symmetric heavy-tailed location-scale t distribution, approaching a Gaussian as freedom grows.

Definition / convention: f(x)=Γ((ν+1)/2)/(scale·sqrt(νπ)Γ(ν/2)) · [1+((x−location)/scale)²/ν]^(−(ν+1)/2).

Arguments / value: freedom=ν>0; scale>0; location and x are real.

Important: Scale is not the standard deviation: Var[X]=scale²·ν/(ν−2) only for ν>2. The mean needs ν>1. This precheck is not proof of numerical convergence, finite moments, finite precision, or support of every operation. Prefer the finite, nondegenerate model conditions given here, even where the library accepts a limiting case.

FunctionInfo.Title: Student t — Probability density f(x)
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real StudentT.PDF(real location, real scale, real freedom, real x)

Probability density f(x). A symmetric heavy-tailed location-scale t distribution, approaching a Gaussian as freedom grows.

Definition / convention: f(x)=Γ((ν+1)/2)/(scale·sqrt(νπ)Γ(ν/2)) · [1+((x−location)/scale)²/ν]^(−(ν+1)/2).

Arguments / value: freedom=ν>0; scale>0; location and x are real. Evaluate at x; the support is specified above.

Important: Scale is not the standard deviation: Var[X]=scale²·ν/(ν−2) only for ν>2. The mean needs ν>1. A density is not P(X=x): point probability is zero for a continuous law. Integrate the density over an interval to obtain a probability.

Example: StudentT.CDF(0,1,3,0) = 0.5.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Student t — Natural logarithm of probability density f(x)

FunctionInfo.Title: Student t — One random draw
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax

Definition / convention: f(x)=Γ((ν+1)/2)/(scale·sqrt(νπ)Γ(ν/2)) · [1+((x−location)/scale)²/ν]^(−(ν+1)/2).

Arguments / value: freedom=ν>0; scale>0; location and x are real. Uses the library’s default random source; no explicit seed is accepted by this overload.

Important: Scale is not the standard deviation: Var[X]=scale²·ν/(ν−2) only for ν>2. The mean needs ν>1. Sample values are random, not the density/CDF evaluated at the parameters. FunctionInfo.Title: Discrete data transform
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
Complex[] Transform(Complex[] functionPoints, string transformate)
Double[] Transform(Double[] functionPoints, string transformate)

Applies a named transform to an array of equally spaced samples.

Arguments / value: Case-sensitive names: FFT, IFFT, DST, IDST, DCT, IDCT, DHT, FHT and IFHT. FHT here means Hilbert transform; DHT means Hartley.

Important: Important overload differences: real FFT/IFFT uses Accord DFT and discards the imaginary result; complex FFT/IFFT uses Math.NET defaults and mutates the input array. Several real transforms also mutate input. The complex DCT/IDCT/DHT conversion currently indexes a rectangular array using its total element count and can throw for nonempty input. Complex FHT/IFHT starts from only the real component. Do not assume every overload is an invertible copy-producing transform.

FunctionInfo.Title: Triangular — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real Triangular.CDF(real lower, real upper, real mode, real x)

Returns F(x)=P(X≤x), the accumulated probability through x. A bounded piecewise-linear density rising to a mode and then falling to zero.

Definition / convention: f(x)=2(x−lower)/[(upper−lower)(mode−lower)] left of mode; 2(upper−x)/[(upper−lower)(upper−mode)] right of it.

Arguments / value: lower<upper, lower≤mode≤upper; support [lower,upper]. Endpoint modes use one-sided limiting formulas.

Important: The mode need not be the midpoint. Equal lower/upper is a degenerate limit, not the displayed ordinary density. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one.

FunctionInfo.Title: Weibull — Cumulative probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real Weibull.CDF(real shape, real scale, real x)

Returns F(x)=P(X≤x), the accumulated probability through x. A positive lifetime model whose hazard decreases, is constant, or increases according to the shape.

Definition / convention: f(x)=(shape/scale)·(x/scale)^(shape−1)·exp(−(x/scale)^shape), x≥0.

Arguments / value: shape>0, scale>0. Shape 1 gives Exponential(rate=1/scale).

Important: Use shape,scale in that order. Scale is a lifetime scale, not a rate. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one.

Example: Weibull.CDF(1,2,2) = 1−exp(−1).

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Weibull — Estimate distribution parameters
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax

Fits a distribution object to the supplied sample sequence. A positive lifetime model whose hazard decreases, is constant, or increases according to the shape.

Definition / convention: f(x)=(shape/scale)·(x/scale)^(shape−1)·exp(−(x/scale)^shape), x≥0.

Arguments / value: samples is a finite, nonempty data sequence; randomSource configures subsequent draws, not the fitting data. Use enough nondegenerate observations to estimate the spread.

Important: Use shape,scale in that order. Scale is a lifetime scale, not a rate. Use positive lifetime observations. Fitting is numerical and can fail for invalid or degenerate samples; it is not a goodness-of-fit test.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

Arguments / value: shape>0, scale>0. Shape 1 gives Exponential(rate=1/scale).

FunctionInfo.Title: Weibull — Probability density f(x)

Definition / convention: f(x)=(shape/scale)·(x/scale)^(shape−1)·exp(−(x/scale)^shape), x≥0.

Arguments / value: shape>0, scale>0. Shape 1 gives Exponential(rate=1/scale). Evaluate at x; the support is specified above.

Important: Use shape,scale in that order. Scale is a lifetime scale, not a rate. A density is not P(X=x): point probability is zero for a continuous law. Integrate the density over an interval to obtain a probability.

Example: Weibull.CDF(1,2,2) = 1−exp(−1).

Returns a Boolean indicating whether the parameter set passes the library’s validity check; it does not compute a sample or a probability. A distribution over symmetric positive-definite scatter matrices.

Definition / convention: For integer ν: X=Σ[j=1..ν] zⱼzⱼᵀ with independent zⱼ~Normal(0,scale); E[X]=ν·scale.

Arguments / value: scale is a real d×d symmetric positive-definite matrix; degreesOfFreedom=ν>d−1 gives a nonsingular law.

Important: A sample is a matrix, not an elementwise independent collection of gamma draws. The library’s parameter precheck is not a substitute for matrix positive definiteness. Prefer the finite, nondegenerate model conditions given here, even where the library accepts a limiting case.

Definition / convention: Rₙᵐ(ρ)=Σₛ₌₀^((n−m)/2) (−1)ˢ(n−s)!ρ^(n−2s)/[s!((n+m)/2−s)!((n−m)/2−s)!]

Arguments / value: Integers n≥0, 0≤m≤n and 0≤ρ≤1. A nonzero radial polynomial requires n−m even.

Important: No angular sin(mθ)/cos(mθ) factor or unit-RMS optical normalization is included.

Example: ZernikeR(2,0,0) = -1

Syntax
real Zipf.CDF(real s, integer n, real x)

Returns F(x)=P(X≤x), the accumulated probability through x. A truncated rank-frequency distribution with power-law weights over ranks 1 through n.

Definition / convention: P(X=k)=k^(−s)/H(n,s); H(n,s)=Σ[j=1..n]j^(−s).

Arguments / value: s>0 and integer n>0; k=1,…,n.

Important: This is the FINITE n model, not an unbounded zeta distribution; its normalization depends on n. This is the lower tail. An upper-tail probability is 1−F(x), though that subtraction can lose precision near one. For a discrete law, the mathematical CDF is a step function over integer outcomes; use integer x at jumps. Fractional-x behavior must not be used as a continuous interpolation of probability masses.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

Arguments / value: s>0 and integer n>0; k=1,…,n.

Important: This is the FINITE n model, not an unbounded zeta distribution; its normalization depends on n. This precheck is not proof of numerical convergence, finite moments, finite precision, or support of every operation. FunctionInfo.Title: Finite Zipf — One random draw

Syntax

Returns one random draw. A truncated rank-frequency distribution with power-law weights over ranks 1 through n.

Definition / convention: P(X=k)=k^(−s)/H(n,s); H(n,s)=Σ[j=1..n]j^(−s).

Important: This is the FINITE n model, not an unbounded zeta distribution; its normalization depends on n. Sample values are random, not the density/CDF evaluated at the parameters. Definition / convention: artanh(t) = ½ ln((1+t)/(1−t))

Arguments / value: Results are in radians where interpreted as angles. Finite real values require −1<t<1. The endpoints are logarithmic singularities.

Important: Alias of artanh; it uses the same convention.

Example: artanh(0) = 0

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Inverse hyperbolic tangent — complex argument
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
complex artgh(complex z)

The inverse of hyperbolic tangent.

Definition / convention: artanh(t) = ½ ln((1+t)/(1−t))

Arguments / value: Results are in radians where interpreted as angles. Complex z. The implementation uses System.Numerics principal inverse/logarithm/square-root values in the displayed formula; branch cuts and endpoint side matter. It returns one value, not all inverse branches.

Important: Alias of artanh; it uses the same convention.

Example: artanh(0) = 0

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Speed of light in vacuum
FunctionInfo.Description:

real c

Propagation speed of light in vacuum and conversion between time and length.

Definition / convention: c = 299792458 m/s exactly in the SI.

Arguments / value: Unit: m s⁻¹. Stored application value: 299792458.

Important: The short name and SpeedOfLightInVacuum represent the same physical quantity. The stored value is the application’s legacy binary64 value, not a live CODATA lookup or an uncertainty-bearing measurement. Use the cited current NIST/SI definition for precision work; independently stored related constants may not be numerically consistent.

Reference: physics.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Complex conjugate
FunctionInfo.Description:

Definition / convention: conj(a+i·b)=a−i·b.

Example: conj(3+4i) = 3−4i

FunctionInfo.Title: Convert an input string to a script scalar
FunctionInfo.Description:

T convert<T>(string result)

Converts text using the application’s legacy string/real/complex conversion helper.

Arguments / value: Use T=string, real (double), or complex; numeric parsing uses the invariant decimal point.

Important: The numeric branch boxes a double and casts it to T, so other numeric T such as integer can fail rather than perform a general numeric conversion. Empty/cancelled text can also fail for value types; this is not a TryParse API.

FunctionInfo.Title: Dilogarithm
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real diLog(real x)

A weighted power series continued beyond its disk of convergence.

Definition / convention: Li₂(z)=Σₖ₌₁^∞ zᵏ/k² for |z|<1.

Arguments / value: Real x≤1 in this wrapper; use the complex overload beyond that interval.

Example: diLog(1) ≈ PI*PI/6

FunctionInfo.Title: Dilogarithm
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
complex diLog(complex z)

A weighted power series continued beyond its disk of convergence.

Definition / convention: Li₂(z)=Σₖ₌₁^∞ zᵏ/k² for |z|<1.

Arguments / value: Complex argument; Li₂ has its conventional branch cut from 1 to +∞.

Example: diLog(1) ≈ PI*PI/6

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Dilogarithm
FunctionInfo.Description:

real diLogarithm(real x)

A weighted power series continued beyond its disk of convergence.

FunctionInfo.Title: Digamma — logarithmic derivative of gamma
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real digamma(real x)

The derivative of log Γ, widely used in likelihood equations and harmonic-number identities.

Definition / convention: ψ(z)=Γ′(z)/Γ(z); ψ(n)=Hₙ₋₁−γ for positive integers n.

Arguments / value: Poles at 0,−1,−2,…; use non-pole real or complex arguments.

Important: Alias of psi with the same convention.

Example: psi(1) ≈ -0.5772156649

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Digamma — logarithmic derivative of gamma
FunctionInfo.Description:

FunctionInfo.Title: Drop-wave benchmark
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real dropWave(real x, real y)

A radially symmetric oscillatory optimization surface.

Definition / convention: −[1+cos(12sqrt(x²+y²))]/[2+(x²+y²)/2]

Arguments / value: Real x,y; global minimum −1 at (0,0).

Important: This evaluates a benchmark surface; it does not run an optimizer.

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Euler’s number
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real e

Base of the natural logarithm and the real exponential whose derivative is itself.

Definition / convention: e=Σ(n=0..∞)1/n!=lim(n→∞)(1+1/n)ⁿ.

Arguments / value: Stored application value: 2.718281828459045. Dimensionless.

Important: This mathematical e is not elementary electric charge; use ElementaryCharge for that physical quantity. This is the finite stored binary64 approximation, not an arbitrary-precision evaluation of the defining limit, series or construction.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Error function
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real erf(real x)

The normalized integral of a Gaussian, continued to an entire complex function.

Definition / convention: erf(z)=2/sqrt(PI) ∫₀ᶻ exp(−t²)dt

Arguments / value: Real or complex input; erf(0)=0. For real x, erf(x) lies in [−1,1].

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Error function
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
complex erf(complex z)

The normalized integral of a Gaussian, continued to an entire complex function.

Definition / convention: erf(z)=2/sqrt(PI) ∫₀ᶻ exp(−t²)dt

Arguments / value: Real or complex input; erf(0)=0. For real x, erf(x) lies in [−1,1].

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Standard normal upper-tail probability
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real erfQ(real x)

The probability that a standard normal variable exceeds x.

Definition / convention: Q(x)=1/2·erfc(x/sqrt(2))

Arguments / value: Real x; values lie in [0,1]. erfQ(0)=1/2.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Standard normal density
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real erfZ(real x)

The probability density of a zero-mean, unit-variance Gaussian.

Definition / convention: φ(x)=exp(−x²/2)/sqrt(2PI)

Arguments / value: Real x; a density, not a tail probability. Area over an interval gives a probability.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Complementary error function
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real erfc(real x)

The upper Gaussian integral complementary to erf.

Definition / convention: erfc(z)=1−erf(z)

Arguments / value: Real or complex input. For real x, erfc(x) decreases from 2 to 0.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Complementary error function
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
complex erfc(complex z)

The upper Gaussian integral complementary to erf.

Definition / convention: erfc(z)=1−erf(z)

Arguments / value: Real or complex input. For real x, erfc(x) decreases from 2 to 0.

Important: The complex wrapper subtracts erf(z) from 1, so very small complementary tails may lose relative accuracy.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Exponentially scaled complementary error
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real erfcx(real x)

Removes the leading Gaussian exponential from erfc mathematically.

Definition / convention: erfcx(z)=exp(z²)erfc(z)

Arguments / value: Real or complex input; erfcx(0)=1.

Important: The current wrapper forms erfc(z)/exp(−z²) directly. It can still overflow, underflow or suffer cancellation; do not assume the name guarantees a stabilized scaled algorithm.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Exponentially scaled complementary error
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
complex erfcx(complex z)

Removes the leading Gaussian exponential from erfc mathematically.

Definition / convention: erfcx(z)=exp(z²)erfc(z)

Arguments / value: Real or complex input; erfcx(0)=1.

Important: The current wrapper forms erfc(z)/exp(−z²) directly. It can still overflow, underflow or suffer cancellation; do not assume the name guarantees a stabilized scaled algorithm.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Imaginary error function
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
complex erfi(complex z)

An entire counterpart of erf defined by rotating its argument.

Definition / convention: erfi(z)=−i·erf(i·z)

Arguments / value: Complex input; for real z its mathematical value is real, despite the name.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Exponential
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real exp(real x)

Raises Euler’s number to a real or complex power.

Definition / convention: exp(x+i·y)=exp(x)·(cos(y)+i·sin(y)).

Arguments / value: Finite real or complex argument; large real parts can overflow or underflow.

Example: exp(0) = 1

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Exponential
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
complex exp(complex z)

Raises Euler’s number to a real or complex power.

Definition / convention: exp(x+i·y)=exp(x)·(cos(y)+i·sin(y)).

Arguments / value: Finite real or complex argument; large real parts can overflow or underflow.

Example: exp(0) = 1

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Factorial
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real factorial(real n)

Product of the positive integers up to n, with the empty product equal to one.

Definition / convention: n! = 1·2·…·n; 0!=1.

Arguments / value: Intended for nonnegative integer n. Returns a floating-point approximation and overflows for sufficiently large n.

Important: This loop accepts a real n: fractional n is effectively truncated by the loop and negative n returns 1. It is not Γ(n+1) analytic continuation; use gamma explicitly for that.

Example: factorial(5) = 120

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Faddeeva complex probability function
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
complex faddeeva(complex z)

A complex Gaussian-response function used in Voigt line profiles and wave propagation.

Definition / convention: w(z)=exp(−z²)erfc(−i·z)

Arguments / value: Complex z; w is entire. This is not simply erf(z) or a real probability.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Bracketed scalar root search
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real findRoot(function f, real a, real b)

Attempts to find a zero of the supplied real function within [a,b].

Definition / convention: Find x such that f(x)=0.

Arguments / value: Supply a callable f and finite endpoints with a<b that bracket a continuous root.

Important: This convenience wrapper fixes accuracy at 0.01 and maximum iterations at 10,000, catches solver exceptions and returns NaN on failure. Use FunctionRoot methods when you need explicit controls.

Example: findRoot(x => x*x-2,0,2) ≈ 1.414 (within the requested accuracy)

Reference: numerics.mathdotnet.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Legacy gravitational acceleration
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real g

A stored near-Earth acceleration used in elementary mechanics.

Definition / convention: F=m·g; free-fall distance from rest is ½g·t².

Arguments / value: Unit: m s⁻². Stored application value: 9.80625.

Important: The stored 9.80625 is NOT the conventional standard acceleration 9.80665. Use StandardAccelerationOfGravity for the conventional value; local gravity varies with location. The stored value is the application’s legacy binary64 value, not a live CODATA lookup or an uncertainty-bearing measurement. Use the cited current NIST/SI definition for precision work; independently stored related constants may not be numerically consistent.

Reference: physics.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Upper incomplete gamma
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real gamma(real a, real x)

The tail of the gamma integral, without division by Γ(a).

Definition / convention: Γ(a,x)=∫ₓ^∞ t^(a−1)exp(−t) dt

Arguments / value: Real a>0 and x≥0; other inputs are rejected by this wrapper.

Important: Do not confuse this with the lower incomplete gamma or the normalized tails gammaP/gammaQ.

Example: gamma(1,2) ≈ exp(-2)

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Gamma function
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real gamma(real x)

The meromorphic extension of the factorial relation to noninteger arguments.

Definition / convention: Γ(z)=∫₀^∞ t^(z−1)e^(−t) dt for Re(z)>0; Γ(z+1)=zΓ(z).

Arguments / value: Simple poles at 0,−1,−2,…; finite negative nonintegers are defined by continuation. Large magnitudes may overflow.

Important: Γ(n)=(n−1)!, not n!. The complex gamma function is single-valued away from its poles.

Example: gamma(5) = 24

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Gamma function — complex argument
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
complex gamma(complex z)

The meromorphic extension of the factorial relation to noninteger arguments.

Definition / convention: Γ(z)=∫₀^∞ t^(z−1)e^(−t) dt for Re(z)>0; Γ(z+1)=zΓ(z).

Arguments / value: Simple poles at 0,−1,−2,…; finite negative nonintegers are defined by continuation. Large magnitudes may overflow.

Important: Γ(n)=(n−1)!, not n!. The complex gamma function is single-valued away from its poles.

Example: gamma(5) = 24

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Lower regularized gamma
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real gammaP(real a, real x)

The accumulated lower gamma-integral fraction, also a gamma-distribution tail.

Definition / convention: P(a,x)=∫₀ˣ t^(a−1)e^(−t)dt/Γ(a)

Arguments / value: Use a>0 and x≥0; results then lie in [0,1]. P(a,x)+Q(a,x)=1.

Important: The second argument is the integration limit, not a scale parameter.

Example: P(1,0)=0 in this convention.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Upper regularized gamma
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real gammaQ(real a, real x)

The remaining upper gamma-integral fraction, also a gamma-distribution tail.

Definition / convention: Q(a,x)=∫ₓ^∞ t^(a−1)e^(−t)dt/Γ(a)

Arguments / value: Use a>0 and x≥0; results then lie in [0,1]. P(a,x)+Q(a,x)=1.

Important: gammaQ delegates to Math.NET and also admits its a=0 limiting convention; the other wrappers require a>0. The second argument is the integration limit, not a scale parameter.

Example: Q(1,0)=1 in this convention.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Greatest common divisor
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real gcd(integer a, integer b)

The largest positive integer dividing both integer inputs.

Definition / convention: gcd(a,b) divides a and b; gcd(12,18)=6.

Arguments / value: Use positive integers for this implementation.

Important: The wrapper returns NaN if either input is zero, rather than the common gcd(a,0)=|a| convention; its Euclidean loop does not normalize negative inputs.

Example: gcd(12,18) = 6

Reference: github.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Planck constant — short name
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real h

Relates photon energy to ordinary frequency, E=h·ν.

Definition / convention: h = 6.62607015×10⁻³⁴ J·s exactly in the modern SI.

Arguments / value: Unit: J s. Stored application value: 6.626069572899999E-34.

Important: This short name and PlanckConstant have different historical stored approximations. Neither should be treated as the current exact SI value. The stored value is the application’s legacy binary64 value, not a live CODATA lookup or an uncertainty-bearing measurement. Use the cited current NIST/SI definition for precision work; independently stored related constants may not be numerically consistent.

Reference: physics.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Standard normal hazard function
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real hazard(real x)

The Gaussian density divided by the remaining upper-tail probability.

Definition / convention: h(x)=φ(x)/Q(x)

Arguments / value: Real x. This is the normal hazard or inverse Mills ratio, not a probability bounded by 1.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Imaginary unit
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
complex i

The complex number whose real part is zero and imaginary part is one.

Definition / convention: i²=−1.

Arguments / value: Stored application value: 0 + 1i. Dimensionless.

Important: System.Numerics.Complex value, distinct from a user’s local loop variable with the same name.

Reference: learn.microsoft.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Matrix inverse
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
Matrix inv<T>(Matrix M)

Returns the inverse of a nonsingular square matrix.

Definition / convention: M·inv(M)≈I

Arguments / value: Square nonsingular matrix.

Important: For a linear system, solving directly is generally preferable to explicitly forming the inverse; ill-conditioning amplifies error.

Reference: github.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Inverse error function
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real inverseErf(real x)

Solves erf(y)=x on the real principal inverse.

Definition / convention: erf(inverseErf(x))=x

Arguments / value: Mathematical domain −1≤x≤1; this wrapper accepts ONLY 0≤x≤1. The endpoint x=1 corresponds to +∞.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Inverse complementary error
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real inverseErfc(real x)

Solves erfc(y)=x on the real principal inverse.

Definition / convention: erfc(inverseErfc(x))=x

Arguments / value: Mathematical domain 0≤x≤2; this wrapper accepts ONLY 0≤x≤1. x=0 corresponds to +∞ and x=1 gives 0.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Hermitian-symmetry predicate
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
bool isHermitian<T>(Matrix M)

Tests equality with the conjugate transpose.

Definition / convention: M=Mᴴ

Arguments / value: A matrix to compare with its conjugate transpose.

Important: Hermitian matrices have real diagonal entries; floating-point equality follows Math.NET’s predicate.

Reference: github.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Approximate identity-pattern predicate
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
bool isIndentity<T>(Matrix M)

Compares the matrix with an identity-pattern matrix of the same shape.

Definition / convention: M≈IdentityMatrix(M)

Arguments / value: Uses relative comparison tolerance 1e−10.

Important: The public identifier is spelled isIndentity. Rectangular diagonal-one matrices can also pass; this does not enforce squareness.

Reference: github.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Primality predicate
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
bool isPrime(integer n)

Tests whether an integer is a prime: a positive integer greater than one with exactly two positive divisors.

Definition / convention: Prime n has no positive divisor other than 1 and n.

Arguments / value: Integers; nonpositive numbers and 1 are not prime.

Example: isPrime(13) = true

Reference: github.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Symmetry predicate
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
bool isSymmetric<T>(Matrix M)

Tests equality with the ordinary transpose.

Definition / convention: M=Mᵀ

Arguments / value: A matrix to compare with its transpose.

Important: For complex matrices this is symmetry, not Hermitian symmetry.

Reference: github.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Approximate row-unitarity predicate
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
bool isUnitary<T>(Matrix M)

Checks the product with the conjugate transpose against identity.

Definition / convention: M·Mᴴ≈I, using the isIndentity tolerance 1e−10.

Arguments / value: A square matrix satisfying this condition is unitary (orthogonal when real).

Important: The wrapper does not require a square matrix, so rectangular matrices with orthonormal rows can also pass.

Reference: github.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Kernel or null-space basis
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
Vector`1[] ker<T>(Matrix M)

Returns basis vectors annihilated by the matrix.

Definition / convention: M·v≈0 for every returned basis vector v.

Arguments / value: Real or complex matrix; returns an array of vectors, possibly empty.

Important: The basis is not unique and numerical rank thresholds affect its dimension.

Reference: github.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Least common multiple
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real lcm(integer a, integer b)

The smallest positive integer divisible by both positive integer inputs.

Definition / convention: lcm(a,b)=a·b/gcd(a,b).

Arguments / value: Use positive integers. The intermediate integer product can overflow.

Important: The wrapper returns NaN if either argument is zero; it does not implement the conventional zero least-common-multiple value.

Example: lcm(4,6) = 12

Reference: github.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Lower regularized gamma
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real leftRegularizedGamma(real a, real x)

The accumulated lower gamma-integral fraction, also a gamma-distribution tail.

Definition / convention: P(a,x)=∫₀ˣ t^(a−1)e^(−t)dt/Γ(a)

Arguments / value: Use a>0 and x≥0; results then lie in [0,1]. P(a,x)+Q(a,x)=1.

Important: The second argument is the integration limit, not a scale parameter.

Example: P(1,0)=0 in this convention.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Dynamic resizable list
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
T list()

Creates an empty list.

Arguments / value: Use zero-based indexing. Elements are dynamic objects; numerical matrix operations require a separate matrix conversion.

Important: A list can grow; its Count is not a matrix row count.

Reference: github.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Typed resizable list
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
List`1 list<T>()

Creates an empty list.

Arguments / value: Use zero-based indexing. The type parameter specifies the element type.

Important: A list can grow; its Count is not a matrix row count.

Reference: github.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Typed resizable list
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
List`1 list<T>(T elements1, T elements2, ...)

Collects the supplied elements in order.

Arguments / value: Use zero-based indexing. The type parameter specifies the element type.

Important: A list can grow; its Count is not a matrix row count.

Reference: github.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Natural logarithm
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real ln(real x)

Logarithm to base e; inverse of the real exponential.

Definition / convention: ln(exp(x))=x.

Arguments / value: Finite real domain x>0; x=0 gives −∞. Complex input uses the principal logarithm, with imaginary part given by the principal argument.

Example: ln(e) ≈ 1

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Natural logarithm
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
complex ln(complex z)

Logarithm to base e; inverse of the real exponential.

Definition / convention: ln(exp(x))=x.

Arguments / value: Finite real domain x>0; x=0 gives −∞. Complex input uses the principal logarithm, with imaginary part given by the principal argument.

FunctionInfo.Title: Logarithm to a supplied base
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real log(real x, real y)

Returns the logarithm of the FIRST argument in the base supplied as the SECOND argument.

Definition / convention: log(x,y)=ln(x)/ln(y).

Arguments / value: Real x>0, base y>0 and y≠1. Complex z uses its principal logarithm divided by the logarithm of the real base.

Example: log(8,2) = 3

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Logarithm to a supplied base
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
complex log(complex z, real nbase)

Returns the logarithm of the FIRST argument in the base supplied as the SECOND argument.

Definition / convention: log(x,y)=ln(x)/ln(y).

Arguments / value: Real x>0, base y>0 and y≠1. Complex z uses its principal logarithm divided by the logarithm of the real base.

Example: log(8,2) = 3

FunctionInfo.Title: Common logarithm
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real log10(real x)

Logarithm to base ten.

Definition / convention: log10(t)=ln(t)/ln(10).

Arguments / value: Real argument positive, or complex argument interpreted through its principal logarithm.

Example: log10(100) = 2

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Common logarithm
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
complex log10(complex z)

Logarithm to base ten.

Definition / convention: log10(t)=ln(t)/ln(10).

Arguments / value: Real argument positive, or complex argument interpreted through its principal logarithm.

Example: log10(100) = 2

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Binary logarithm
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real log2(real x)

Logarithm to base two.

Definition / convention: log2(t)=ln(t)/ln(2).

Arguments / value: Real argument positive, or complex argument interpreted through its principal logarithm.

Example: log2(8) = 3

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Binary logarithm
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
complex log2(complex z)

Logarithm to base two.

Definition / convention: log2(t)=ln(t)/ln(2).

Arguments / value: Real argument positive, or complex argument interpreted through its principal logarithm.

Example: log2(8) = 3

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Logarithm of modified Bessel K
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real logBesselKν(real ν, real x)

Computes ln K_ν(x) without requiring a representable unscaled K value.

Definition / convention: ln[K_ν(x)]

Arguments / value: Real ν≥0 and x>0 in this wrapper; otherwise NaN.

Important: K is positive for this domain. This logarithm is distinct from a scaled K function.

Reference: www.gnu.org

FunctionInfo.Title: Natural logarithm of beta
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real logBeta(real a, real b)

A numerically useful logarithmic form of the positive beta function.

Definition / convention: ln B(a,b)=lnΓ(a)+lnΓ(b)−lnΓ(a+b)

Arguments / value: Real a>0,b>0 in this wrapper.

Example: logBeta(1,1) = 0

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Logarithm of the complementary error function
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real logErfc(real x)

Computes the Gaussian-tail logarithm directly rather than taking a logarithm after tail underflow.

Definition / convention: ln(erfc(x))

Arguments / value: Real x; useful for likelihoods involving small Gaussian tails.

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Logarithm of gamma
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real logGamma(real x)

Evaluates log Γ without first forming a possibly overflowing gamma value.

Definition / convention: exp(LogΓ(z))=Γ(z) away from poles, with the library’s continuous branch convention.

Arguments / value: Real x>0 only in this wrapper; x≤0 returns NaN.

Important: A complex log-gamma value need not equal the principal logarithm of a separately rounded complex gamma value.

Example: logGamma(1) = 0

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Logarithm of gamma — complex argument
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
complex logGamma(complex z)

Evaluates log Γ without first forming a possibly overflowing gamma value.

Definition / convention: exp(LogΓ(z))=Γ(z) away from poles, with the library’s continuous branch convention.

Arguments / value: This wrapper rejects Re(z)<0 even though complex log-gamma has a larger mathematical continuation. Poles and branch conventions remain relevant.

Important: A complex log-gamma value need not equal the principal logarithm of a separately rounded complex gamma value.

Example: logGamma(1) = 0

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Logarithm of gamma
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real logΓ(real x)

Evaluates log Γ without first forming a possibly overflowing gamma value.

Definition / convention: exp(LogΓ(z))=Γ(z) away from poles, with the library’s continuous branch convention.

Arguments / value: Real x>0 only in this wrapper; x≤0 returns NaN.

Important: Alias of logGamma with the same convention. A complex log-gamma value need not equal the principal logarithm of a separately rounded complex gamma value.

Example: logGamma(1) = 0

FunctionInfo.Title: Logarithm of gamma — complex argument
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
complex logΓ(complex z)

Evaluates log Γ without first forming a possibly overflowing gamma value.

Definition / convention: exp(LogΓ(z))=Γ(z) away from poles, with the library’s continuous branch convention.

Arguments / value: This wrapper rejects Re(z)<0 even though complex log-gamma has a larger mathematical continuation. Poles and branch conventions remain relevant.

FunctionInfo.Description:

FunctionInfo.Title: Dense matrix from a rectangular array
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
Matrix matrix(Complex[,] array)
Matrix matrix(Double[,] array)
Matrix matrix(Int32[,] array)
T matrix(Object[,] array)

Copies a rectangular two-dimensional array into a Math.NET real or complex dense matrix.

Definition / convention: M[row,column] corresponds to array[row,column]; indices start at zero.

Arguments / value: Integer arrays become real matrices; real and complex arrays retain that numerical domain. The dynamic array overload chooses complex if it finds a complex element.

Important: Dynamic elements must be convertible to the chosen scalar type. A matrix is not a jagged array; rows must have consistent lengths.

Reference: github.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Zero-filled matrix
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
Matrix matrix<T>(integer n, integer m)

Allocates a dense matrix of the requested size.

Definition / convention: matrix<T>(n,m): n rows, m columns; vector<T>(n): n elements.

Arguments / value: Nonnegative dimensions within available memory; library-specific zero-size constraints apply.

Important: For generic numeric matrix creation use T=real (double) or T=complex. The wrapper’s attempted cast for other numeric T can return null; the generic-looking name is not a guarantee of all scalar types.

Reference: github.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Rectangular submatrix — legacy minor name
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
Matrix minor<T>(Matrix M, integer i, integer j, integer m, integer n)

Extracts a contiguous block, not a determinant or cofactor.

Definition / convention: Rows i,…,i+m−1; columns j,…,j+n−1.

Arguments / value: i,j are zero-based starting indices; m,n are row/column counts within M.

Important: Despite the name, this does not remove a row/column and does not compute a signed minor.

Reference: github.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Greatest common divisor
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real nwd(integer a, integer b)

The largest positive integer dividing both integer inputs.

Definition / convention: gcd(a,b) divides a and b; gcd(12,18)=6.

Arguments / value: Use positive integers for this implementation.

Important: Alias of gcd; it uses the same convention. The wrapper returns NaN if either input is zero, rather than the common gcd(a,0)=|a| convention; its Euclidean loop does not normalize negative inputs.

Example: gcd(12,18) = 6

Reference: github.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Least common multiple
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real nww(integer a, integer b)

The smallest positive integer divisible by both positive integer inputs.

Definition / convention: lcm(a,b)=a·b/gcd(a,b).

Arguments / value: Use positive integers. The intermediate integer product can overflow.

Important: Alias of lcm; it uses the same convention. The wrapper returns NaN if either argument is zero; it does not implement the conventional zero least-common-multiple value.

Example: lcm(4,6) = 12

Important: This opens a modal Windows plot dialog; it does not return an image or implement server-side rendering. Browser users should use the Chart screen. Data-series orientation follows the historical AddDataPoints adapters, and mismatched sequence lengths can fail.

FunctionInfo.Title: Polygamma of integer order
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real polyGamma(integer n, real x)

The n-th derivative of the digamma function.

Definition / convention: ψ⁽ⁿ⁾(x)=dⁿ⁺¹ lnΓ(x)/dxⁿ⁺¹; ψ⁽⁰⁾=ψ.

Arguments / value: Integer n≥0; avoid gamma poles in x. n=1 is trigamma, n=2 tetragamma.

Example: polyGamma(1,1) ≈ PI*PI/6

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Digamma — logarithmic derivative of gamma
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real polyGamma(real x)

The derivative of log Γ, widely used in likelihood equations and harmonic-number identities.

Definition / convention: ψ(z)=Γ′(z)/Γ(z); ψ(n)=Hₙ₋₁−γ for positive integers n.

Arguments / value: Poles at 0,−1,−2,…; use non-pole real or complex arguments.

Important: The one-argument polyGamma/ψn/ψⁿ names mean order zero, i.e. digamma, not trigamma.

Example: psi(1) ≈ -0.5772156649

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Power
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
complex pow(complex x, complex y)
real pow(real x, real y)

Raises the first argument to the second. The real and complex overloads share this completion signature.

Definition / convention: pow(x,y)=xʸ; for nonzero complex x, exp(y·Log(x)).

Arguments / value: Real negative bases with nonintegral exponents can produce NaN. The complex overload selects a branch, not all possible powers.

Example: pow(2,3) = 8

Reference: dlmf.nist.gov

FunctionInfo.Title: Integer matrix power
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
Matrix pow<T>(Matrix M, integer n)

Raises a square matrix to an integer power using matrix multiplication.

Definition / convention: M⁰=I; M⁻ⁿ=(M⁻¹)ⁿ for n>0.

Arguments / value: Square M; negative n requires invertibility. Exclude the most-negative 32-bit integer because Math.Abs(n) overflows.

Important: This is not an elementwise power.

Reference: github.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Numeric primality flag
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
integer prime(real x)

A numeric wrapper around isPrime, useful in expressions that need a 0/1 indicator.

Definition / convention: prime(x)=1 if the converted integer is prime; otherwise 0.

Arguments / value: The wrapper returns −1 when x<1; otherwise it casts x to a 32-bit integer.

Important: This does not return the x-th prime. Use integral values in the integer range; fractions are truncated.

Example: prime(13) = 1

Reference: github.com

The derivative of log Γ, widely used in likelihood equations and harmonic-number identities.

Definition / convention: ψ(z)=Γ′(z)/Γ(z); ψ(n)=Hₙ₋₁−γ for positive integers n.

Arguments / value: Poles at 0,−1,−2,…; use non-pole real or complex arguments.

The derivative of log Γ, widely used in likelihood equations and harmonic-number identities.

FunctionInfo.Title: Uniform random value from zero
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real random(integer x)
real random(real x)

Generates a pseudorandom real or integer-valued result according to overload selection.

Definition / convention: Real x: x·U; integer x: an integer from 0 THROUGH x; U∈[0,1).

Arguments / value: The generator changes state on each sample; repeated calls need not agree.

Important: Use real x≥0 for [0,x), integer x≥0 for the inclusive integer range. Negative integer x returns NaN. Integer MaxValue cannot safely be used because the implementation adds 1.

Reference: github.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Uniform random value between bounds
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
real random(integer x, integer y)
real random(real x, real y)

Generates a pseudorandom value between two supplied bounds.

Definition / convention: Real x,y: x+(y−x)U; integer x,y: an integer from x THROUGH y; U∈[0,1).

Arguments / value: The generator changes state on each sample; repeated calls need not agree.

Important: Use x≤y. The real and integer overloads differ at the upper endpoint; both are returned as real numbers. Integer MaxValue as y overflows the y+1 bound.

Reference: github.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Random point in a complex rectangle
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
complex random(complex z)

Independently samples the real and imaginary coordinates between zero and the respective components of z.

Definition / convention: Re(z)·U+i·Im(z)·V, with independent uniform U,V∈[0,1).

Arguments / value: The generator changes state on each sample; repeated calls need not agree.

Important: This fills an axis-aligned rectangle, not a disk. Negative components reverse the direction of the corresponding interval.

Reference: github.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Random point on a complex line segment
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
complex random(complex z1, complex z2)

Samples a single interpolation factor between two complex endpoints.

Definition / convention: z₁+(z₂−z₁)U, with uniform U∈[0,1).

Arguments / value: The generator changes state on each sample; repeated calls need not agree.

Important: This samples a LINE SEGMENT, not independent coordinates in a rectangle; z₂ is normally excluded by the half-open random factor.

Reference: github.com

FunctionInfo.Title: Numerical matrix rank
FunctionInfo.Description:
Syntax
integer rank<T>(Matrix M)

Estimates the number of linearly independent columns/rows.

Definition / convention: rank(M)≤min(rows,columns)

Arguments / value: A real or complex matrix; numerical rank depends on a singular-value threshold.

Important: Not an exact symbolic rank for nearly dependent data.

Reference: github.com
